title: History, SCDs and snapshots
summary: How to keep the past queryable: slowly changing dimension types, SCD2 with MERGE and dbt snapshots, bitemporal data and point-in-time joins.

blocks.text: Source systems usually store only the current state: a customer row is overwritten when the customer moves. Analytics needs the past. *Revenue by customer region last year* has two valid answers: by the region the customer was in when they bought, or by the region they are in now. Slowly changing dimension (SCD) techniques let you choose deliberately, per attribute.
9.1 The SCD types

head: Type
Behaviour on change
History kept
Typical use
rows: Date of birth, original signup channel
Typo corrections, attributes nobody analyses historically
Close the current row, insert a new version
Keep current and previous value in two columns
A one-off reorganisation where both old and new mapping are reported
Current table plus separate history table (or mini-dimension)
Fast-changing attributes split from a large dimension
1 + 2 + 3: SCD2 rows plus a current-value column overwritten on all versions
Full, plus current view on every row
Report both as-was and as-is without an extra join
SCD2 dimension plus a durable natural key on the fact for joining to a current view
Same as 6, done through two join paths

blocks.text: Types 1 and 2 cover most real needs. Choose per attribute, not per table: in the same customer dimension, email may be type 1 and segment type 2. Type 6 is popular in BI because analysts get as-was (`segment`) and as-is (`current_segment`) in one row.
9.2 Anatomy of an SCD2 dimension

blocks.title: SCD2 customer dimension (Snowflake SQL)
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key    INTEGER IDENTITY,      -- surrogate, one per version
  customer_id     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- natural/durable key
  customer_name   VARCHAR(200),
  segment         VARCHAR(30),           -- type 2
  region          VARCHAR(30),           -- type 2
  email           VARCHAR(200),          -- type 1
  row_hash        VARCHAR(64),           -- hash of type-2 columns
  valid_from      TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  valid_to        TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL, -- '9999-12-31' when current
  is_current      BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

items: **Half-open intervals**: a version is valid for `valid_from <= t < valid_to`. Closed intervals on both ends create overlaps at the boundary instant.
**High date instead of NULL** for the current row's `valid_to` keeps range predicates simple and index/pruning friendly.
**Row hash** over the tracked columns makes change detection one comparison instead of N null-safe comparisons.
Facts store the surrogate key of the version that was current when the event happened, which makes as-was reporting a plain equi-join.

blocks.text: Comparing columns with `<>` misses changes to or from NULL, because `NULL <> 'x'` is not true. Use a hash of coalesced values, or `IS DISTINCT FROM` where the engine supports it (Snowflake, Postgres and Spark SQL do).
9.3 Implementing SCD2 with MERGE

A single MERGE cannot both update the old version and insert the new version for the same source row, because each source row matches the target once. The standard trick is to feed the MERGE a source that contains changed rows **twice**: once with the real key (to close the old version) and once with a NULL merge key (which never matches, so it is inserted).

blocks.title: SCD2 MERGE with the union trick (Snowflake / Spark SQL style)
blocks.text:
MERGE INTO dim_customer t
USING (
  -- every incoming row, keyed normally
  SELECT s.customer_id AS merge_key, s.*
  FROM stg_customer s
  UNION ALL
  -- changed rows again with a NULL key, forcing an insert
  SELECT NULL AS merge_key, s.*
  FROM stg_customer s
  JOIN dim_customer d
    ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id
   AND d.is_current
  WHERE d.row_hash <> s.row_hash
) src
ON t.customer_id = src.merge_key AND t.is_current
WHEN MATCHED AND t.row_hash <> src.row_hash THEN UPDATE SET
  valid_to   = src.loaded_at,
  is_current = FALSE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (customer_id, customer_name, segment, region, email,
   row_hash, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
VALUES
  (src.customer_id, src.customer_name, src.segment, src.region, src.email,
   src.row_hash, src.loaded_at, '9999-12-31', TRUE);

Brand-new customers fall into the NOT MATCHED branch through the first half of the union. The staging set must contain at most one row per `customer_id`; deduplicate first (chapter 14) or the MERGE will fail or behave nondeterministically. Type-1 columns such as email need a separate UPDATE across all versions of the customer.
9.4 dbt snapshots

dbt snapshots implement SCD2 for you on top of a source table. Each run compares the current source to the snapshot table and closes and inserts versions. dbt adds `dbt_valid_from`, `dbt_valid_to` (NULL for the current row by default), `dbt_scd_id` and `dbt_updated_at`.

blocks.title: snapshots/customers.yml (dbt 1.9+ YAML snapshot config)
blocks.text:
snapshots:
  - name: customers_snapshot
    relation: source('crm', 'customers')
    config:
      schema: snapshots
      unique_key: customer_id
      strategy: timestamp
      updated_at: updated_at
      hard_deletes: invalidate

items: **timestamp strategy**: trusts a reliable `updated_at` column in the source. Cheap and precise.
**check strategy**: compares listed columns (`check_cols`) when no trustworthy timestamp exists. Costlier and blind to changes that revert within one interval.
Snapshots capture only what they see at run time. A value that changes twice between daily runs loses the middle version; CDC (chapter 17) captures every change.

blocks.text: Snapshots are state you cannot rebuild: if the source has no history, a dropped snapshot table is gone forever. Keep them in a protected schema, exclude them from full-refresh jobs and back them up. Older dbt versions configured snapshots in SQL files with a `{% snapshot %}` block; check the documentation for your version.
9.5 Bitemporal modelling
SCD2 as usually built tracks one timeline. Regulated domains need two:

items: **Valid time** (business or effective time): when the fact was true in the real world. *The customer moved on 1 March.*
**Transaction time** (system or recorded time): when the database learned it. *We were told on 20 March.*

blocks.text: With both, you can answer *what did we believe on 15 March about where the customer lived on 10 March?*, which is exactly what an auditor asks when a report published on 15 March is questioned. Corrections never overwrite: a backdated change closes the current belief in transaction time and inserts new rows.

Lakehouse time travel (chapter 23) and Snowflake Time Travel give a limited form of transaction time at table level, but retention is days or weeks, not years, and is not a substitute for modelled bitemporality.
9.6 Point-in-time joins

When facts do not carry the version surrogate key, you join on the natural key and the time range. This is also the core operation for ML feature stores: each training label must see feature values as of the label's timestamp, never later, or the model learns from the future (label leakage).

blocks.title: As-of join with an SCD2 dimension
blocks.text:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.ordered_at,
       c.segment AS segment_at_order_time
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_customer c
  ON  c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  AND o.ordered_at >= c.valid_from
  AND o.ordered_at <  c.valid_to;

Range joins are expensive on distributed engines because they cannot hash on the range. Mitigations: resolve the surrogate key once at load time and store it on the fact, use engine-specific as-of join support where available (Snowflake has `ASOF JOIN`; check the current documentation for your engine), or bucket by day before the range predicate.

blocks.title: Sales commission disputes
blocks.text: A B2B company paid commissions by account territory. Territories were reassigned quarterly and the CRM overwrote them, so last quarter's commission report could not be reproduced. The data team added a dbt snapshot on accounts and stored the territory version key on the bookings fact at load time.
items: A type-6 `current_territory` column served pipeline forecasting without a second join
Two quarters of history were unrecoverable: snapshots only start when you turn them on

blocks.title: Design history for an insurance policy dimension
blocks.text: Policies have a holder, premium tier, coverage level and agent. Underwriters backdate coverage changes by up to 60 days, and regulators can ask what the company reported on any past date. Decide the SCD type for each attribute, whether you need bitemporality, and how claims facts should join to policy versions.
hints: Which question requires transaction time, not just valid time?
What happens to an already-loaded claim when a backdated change arrives?

items: Choose an SCD type per attribute; types 1 and 2 cover most needs, type 6 gives as-was and as-is together.
Use half-open validity intervals, a high end date and a row hash for change detection.
SCD2 MERGE needs the union trick so one changed source row both closes and inserts.
dbt snapshots automate SCD2 but only capture changes visible at run time and cannot be rebuilt.
Bitemporal data separates when something was true from when it was recorded; point-in-time joins prevent leakage.

blocks.q: Finance wants each order reported under the customer segment at order time, and marketing wants every order under the current segment, both from one row. Which SCD type fits best?
blocks.explain: Type 6 keeps SCD2 versions (as-was) plus a current-value column overwritten on every version (as-is). Type 3 only keeps one previous value, not full history.

blocks.q: Why does the SCD2 MERGE pattern union changed rows a second time with a NULL merge key?
options: Because MERGE cannot update timestamp columns
So the changed row is matched once to close the old version and also inserted as a new version
blocks.explain: Each source row matches at most once. The NULL-keyed copy never matches, so it lands in the NOT MATCHED branch and is inserted, while the normally keyed copy closes the old row.

blocks.q: A customer's address changes twice between two daily dbt snapshot runs. What does the snapshot record?
options: An error, because snapshots forbid multiple changes
Only the final state; the intermediate version is lost
blocks.explain: Snapshots compare state at run time, so they see only the final value. Capturing every intermediate change requires CDC from the source log.

blocks.q: An auditor asks what the company believed on 15 March about a customer's region on 10 March. What do you need?
options: Transaction time as well as valid time
Table time travel with default retention
blocks.explain: What we believed at a past moment is transaction (recorded) time; when it was true is valid time. The question needs both. Table time travel retention is usually too short for audits.
